newsitem.title: KENYA: New police commissioner takes over Kenyan force.
newsitem.headline: New police commissioner takes over Kenyan force.

text.p: Kenya's new police commissioner, appointed after police shot dead three students, on Friday took charge of a force suffering from low morale and accused of indiscipline, rampant corruption and brutality.
"Duncan Wachira arrived this morning and is in a handover meeting," said police spokesman Senior Superintendent Peter Kimanthi. Wachira was formerly the police chief for troubled northeastern Kenya.
President Daniel arap Moi's office announced on Thursday that Shedrach Kiruki had retired as police chief one day after police shot dead two students at Nairobi's Kenyatta University.
A dozen policemen were charged in a court on Thursday with the deaths at the university. The men, including a senior officer, were not required to plead but were remanded in custody until January.
The two Kenyatta University students died on Wednesday when police fired as students protested against the fatal shooting by police of a student at Egerton University in Njoro on Tuesday.
Nairobi newspapers on Thursday said the Kenyan police force was inept, poorly equipped and disillusioned and warned Wachira that most ordinary Kenyans feared police officers and avoided them.

The East African Standard newspaper said police appeared to be pawns in a chess game run by crooks and many Kenyans did not bother to call police when they were robbed because either their vehicles had no fuel or officers were frightened to go out.
But the newspaper added that Wachira had risen through the police ranks and become one of the most respected officers.
"Any confidence the population may have that they are protected will evaporate now that the guns seem to be trained on the innocent," said the Daily Nation, urging Wachira to investigate.

A Kenyan human rights group saidn last week there was increasing concern about the number of "suspects" and "wanted criminals" being killed by armed police in circumstances where the only version of the shootings came from police themselves.

A report this month on the crumbling justice system in Kenya by the London-based human rights group African Rights said the police generated widespread fear among the public as they acted primarily in their own interests or under government direction.

"The police as an institution has basically collapsed; demoralised and poorly paid, the force sacrifices professionalism and investigative skills for 'short cut' methods of brutality and corrution," the report said.

"Financing training and education programmes for the police cannot overcome the reality that they are licensed to commit abuses by a political framework of institutions, controlled by the president," it said.
"The Kenyan government is therefore directly responsible for the violence that characterises the police force," it added.
